terms.grammar: conjunction, first in its clause; nec mostly before consonants
evidence: Plin. Ep. 1.15.1: prōmittis ad cēnam, nec venīs?
Cic. Fam. 14.3.5: mihi tē cārius nihil esse nec umquam fuisse
terms.comment: Latin joins the negative to the “and”: not et nōn but nec. So “and nobody” is nec quisquam, “and nothing” nec quicquam, “and never” nec umquam, “and yet not” nec tamen. Et nōn stays where one word is negated against another, as in a contrast.

terms.gloss: and not (in commands, wishes and purpose clauses)
terms.grammar: conjunction, with the subjunctive or imperative
evidence: Cato Agr. 37: cavētō nē quam māteriam dolēs, neu caedās, neu tangās, nisi siccam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The “and not” that continues nē, ut or a command: “and don’t …”, “and so that … not”.

phrases.latin: heus tū! prōmittis ad cēnam, nec venīs?
phrases.english: hey, you! you promise to come to dinner and don’t come?

phrases.latin: nesciō quid nunc tacēs nec muttīs
phrases.english: I don’t know why you are quiet now and don’t say a word

phrases.latin: nīl spernat auris, nec tamen crēdat statim
phrases.english: let the ear scorn nothing, and yet not believe at once

phrases.latin: cūrā ut valeās et ita tibi persuādeās, mihi tē cārius nihil esse nec umquam fuisse
phrases.english: take care of yourself, and be sure that nothing is dearer to me than you, and never has been

phrases.latin: cavētō nē quam māteriam dolēs, neu caedās, neu tangās, nisi siccam
phrases.english: take care not to hew any timber, or cut it, or touch it, unless it is dry
